To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.

This study establishes partial uniform ellipticity for a class of symmetric concave functions defined on a space of closed convex sets in $ \mathbb{R}^n $. The approach involves applying a first-order expansion technique to the Monge-Amp`ere operator defined on the set of convex functions equipped with the $ C^{1, \alpha} $ norm. These symmetrical properties are specifically tailored for non-local regularity analysis of a class of fully nonlinear elliptic equations involving the optimal Wasserstein gradient flow.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With a set of genuine LIGO data spanning two decades, we observe that the network can accurately classify known neutron star and black hole events with high confidence, while displaying low probability for unrelated data chunks. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing deep learning techniques to facilitate the real-time detection of neutron star mergers from gravitational waves.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, this research finds that outdoor diversity experienced a greater decline than indoor diversity, with New York City showing a 10 percentage point lower recovery than Boston, New Orleans, and San Francisco combined. Furthermore, this study suggests that one size does not fit all; policies need to be tailored to each context to promote diversity and its associated benefits, while mitigating inequalities in access to the urban setting.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, a combination of one-dimensional and three-dimensional scenarios can coexist, with the star's growth influenced by the impact of gas and the characteristics of the inner disk. By incorporating the three-dimensional nature, the accretion model predicts observable differences in spectral energy distribution, allowing for testable predictions through observation.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in suboptimal conditions.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing modern language models and overcoming their limitations.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the CyCUDA library, an efficient Cython extension that provides GPU-optimized data structures and memory management while allowing seamless integration with conventional CPU code.  The CyCUDA library includes a collection of pre-built data structures, such as arrays of structures and linked lists, along with memory allocation methods that minimize fragmentation and allow for efficient parallel execution.  To validate the effectiveness of CyCUDA in accelerating complex code that uses conventional data structures and requires parallel memory allocation, we developed several benchmark applications, including a GPU implementation of the Earley parser and a simulated GPU agent-based model.  These applications allow us to evaluate the speed, memory allocation efficiency, and feasibility of using CyCUDA to parallelize conventional object-oriented code, ultimately paving the way for significant performance gains in a broad spectrum of applications.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed calculations of spectra were performed for manganese and cobalt impurities on $s$-wave and d-wave lead-based superconductors, taking advantage of the availability of experimental data for electron-phonia coupling-free systems like manganese- and cobalt-paired lithium-fluoride-doped lead. A direct correlation between the local magnetic moments and the splitting of the spin-down YSR bands was discovered through the research. This study aims to validate the findings through subsequent experimental data.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.53$ days, $51.69$ days, and $84.55$ days. Additionally, there is an candidate super-Earth with an orbital period of $49.46$ days. By calculating their radii, we found they range from $2.46$ to $2.95$ Earth radiitions. Through photometry and spectroscopy, we determined that the planets receive between $41\%$ and $82\%$ of the Earth's incoming solar energy. Due to TOI-712's large observable area, $TESS$ has been able to detect $TOI\text{-}712\ b\ c$ and potentially TOI\text{-}712\ d$ and provides an outstanding opportunity to investigate the evolution of young planets within a billion years.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a slightly higher total energy level than their substitutional counterparts, yet they remain well within the range of vibrational energy.  Notably, due to a large formation energy level, these defects are unlikely to arise under normal conditions, but may well be present in experimental samples with carbon or nitrogen contamination.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. The influence of the target's properties, such as the density of the plasma, as well as the angle and polarization of the emitted particles, further complicates the phenomenon. The findings of the study are particularly useful for positron-based experiments involving high-intensity lasers and have implications for understanding the positrons generated through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.012$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.25{\deg}C resolution, a 1.8{\deg}C maximum error, and an 11{\deg}C temperature range of 0{\deg}C to 70{\deg}C, along with an 8-bit digital output, 50nW power consumption, and a 1.2$mf_p$ capacit

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric structures over Lie groupoids and their transformation via the Chern-Weil process. Starting with an introduction to the necessary background on gauge theory over Lie groupoids, we examine the construction of horizontal connections on two types of bundles - principal bundles associated with Lie algebras and projective principal bundles - through the Chern-Weil process. A key aspect involves demonstrating how the Chern-Weil map respects the quotienting of a nonabelian Lie algebra under a generated ideal. Furthermore, we investigate the generated ideal within a principal bundle over a Lie groupoid, utilizing a slice to establish its relation to a subbundle of the adjoint bundle. Ultimately, we utilize this insight to develop a simplified formula for the generated ideal within a quotient Lie algebra.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this discovery's effect on the established correlation between the mass function and the initial mass function.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computations reveal that as the membrane approaches complete loss of stiffness, initial perturbations lead to periodic or quasi-periodic behavior before transitioning to chaos at a critical point.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for the C5H5 system than for the C6H6 system. The calculated CN over CCH ratio for the aromatic benzene derivative is significantly lower than the ratio for the cyclical cyclopentadiene derivative, which could be attributed to the different ways the molecules are destroyed.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs. A consistent and closed system of equations was established, incorporating a unified dark fluid with nonlinear viscosity, adapted from the work of Zeldovich. By applying a heuristic approach, suitable solutions were found, which successfully reproduce the $\Lambda$CDM behavior at late times. Furthermore, the stability, causality, and thermodynamic properties of the solution were thoroughly examined.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays are highly sensitive to light dark matter with masses near 2 GeV, whereas other particle physics experiments have more stringent limits on neutrino masses around 1 eV.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\exp(-\pi b/\sqrt{x})}{2-\exp(-\pi b/\sqrt{x})}$, L\'evy denotes the normal distribution, and $b$ is the symmetric difference of the random walk's positive and negative tail sums.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires extensive work to segment individual cells from histological images. Although several nucleus segmentation models have been proposed, training these models is made exponentially more difficult by the scarcity of labeled data. Self-supervised learning has been reported to mitigate this issue effectively, yet current methods focus primarily on whole-image pathologies and fail to generate cell-level representations. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework called SS-NucType, a combination of a self-supervised generative network and a variational nucleus type representation learning module. In this design, the former network utilizes unusual pairing techniques and an adversarial autoencoder component to generate a generative model capable of reconstructing images, whereas the latter module captures various features associated with specific diseases by analyzing labeled data only once, and then reuses the trained nucleus type representation to guide the initial network in obtaining more meaningful representation learning without labels. Experimental evaluations on three publicly available datasets confirm the superior performance of our model in comparison to the current leading methods.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that they can be viewed as conventional CNNs that operate on the spectrum of frequencies defined by the graph's structure. A visual representation of the GCNN architecture and its components is also presented to facilitate a clear comprehension of the network's operations and the learning process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters of the scalar field. The equation defining these parameters has distinct solutions, each associated with a different Chern-Simons theory. To find a unique solution, additional constraints must be imposed; otherwise, the solution space is too broad. The paper explores this issue by imposing conditions that require connections to have trivial holonomy along specific paths, effectively constraining the theory to a set of non-degenerate matter fields known as conformal scalar singlets. The path to implementing these constraints involves exploring the phase space of the Chern-Simons theory, which can be done using geometric methods involving coadjoint orbits. The result of this exploration is the identification of the theory's valid configuration space as a two-dimensional manifold of geometric properties. The scalar field's action is then replaced with an induced action based on this manifold, from which the equations of motion for the general case are derived. The induced action for a point particle demonstrates that its trajectory aligns with a geodesic in this geometric manifold. The properties of conformal scalar singlets and massless complex scalars are also explored and compared in this analysis.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial symmetry. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its natural counterpart; however, its limited transmit beam's breadth restricts elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique proposes utilizing wide lateral resolution while preserving the high sampling rate and amplitude response of a single transducer element. The proposed method involves transmitting a single pulse from one transducer element and receiving the echo through the entire array's aperture width, effectively. The method is validated through both simulations and in-vivo experiments using high-frequency multi-element ultrasound probes, demonstrating the theoretical benefits of VSSA through elastograms produced from real-time ultrasound data acquired at multiple channels and frequencies, effectively.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey of multiple approaches to calculating lepton-to-weak boson transition form factors is also conducted to analyze their applications to 2-to-n particle interactions in both coherent and incoherent regimes. A comparison of predictions made by different approaches is made to identify any discrepancies. A summary of potential approaches to re-summing power-law corrections in the distribution functions is also provided. A comparison of the relevance of weak boson distribution functions at different particle interaction stages, specifically at 3-to-3 and 4-to-2 particle scattering, is made to demonstrate the application of weak boson distribution functions in such interactions. A final estimate of weak boson distribution functions is provided for a 10 TeV polarized polarized muon collider operating at its design luminosity through both coherent and incoherent contributions from W and Z particle emission.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's innovation of parametric THH, it is demonstrated that parametric THH corresponds to the homological equivalent of the shadow of the bicategory associated with a stable infinity category. Moreover, this equivalence, when applied to the bicategory derived from rings in the context of classical THH, yields a connection between the homology of the shadow of this bicategory and the free loop space of the classifying space (result established in [Ber15]).

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically selects challenging samples for training, resulting in the creation of two network components: one to identify challenging samples and another to re-rank image areas, focused on those elements. Our approach, which requires no sound information and is trained solely on visual data, demonstrates superior performance compared to other methods that use visual/audio alignment training and manual easy/hard sample labeling, according to multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, our method that uses no sound information but is trained on visual data alone, outperforms several state-of-the-art methods that rely on visual/audio joint training.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a basis for a potential individual economic policy.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields a set of non-propagating ghost modes associated with a harmonic coordinate condition.  These modes interact with a specific non-propagating component of the gravitational field source, creating an inconsistency that hints at the rigidity of the harmonic gauge and suggests that general relativity cannot be viewed merely as a theory of perturbations on a static background metric.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and total energy. The degree of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing is heavily influenced by the balance between spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions, with possible non-trivial implications for experimental results. The absence of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ configuration mixing in standard Hund's rules based explanations and many density functional theory implementations, we highlight, could lead to the misinterpretation of experimental data, as demonstrated with the case of oxypnictides.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, yet real-world examples are scarce due to the GAN's black-box nature and complexity. In this study, a medical imaging technique utilizing the style-based generator alternative, which functions as a white-box generator capable of producing high-fidelity images, was leveraged to investigate potential uses with medical images. Specifically, a sequence of demonstrations has been presented involving the generation of pediatric pneumonia chest X-rays from healthy X-ray styles and extraction of a pneumonia style from existing X-rays. Furthermore, a pediatric pneumonia style was generated and inserted into the extraction task, as well as a hidden emphysema style was created without actual disease data. Despite its limitations, this work using the style-based GAGAN demonstrates effective medical imaging styles that go beyond surface-level features, as confirmed by both visual and radiological assessments.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
